title: How Blood Travels Through Your Body
summary: How the heart, arteries, veins, and capillaries work together to move blood, oxygen, and nutrients through your body.
poll: The heart and blood vessels are the body's hardest workers.

versions.title: Blood on the Move
versions.text:
Touch your wrist. Feel a beat? That is blood.

Your heart pumps blood. It is like a fist. It never stops.

Blood moves in tubes. We call them vessels. They go all through you.

Some tubes take blood away from the heart. We call them arteries. They have thick walls.

Other tubes bring blood back to the heart. We call them veins.

Tiny tubes are called capillaries. They are thin as hair. Here, blood gives food and air to cells. It picks up trash too.

Blood goes to the lungs. It gets fresh air there. Then it goes back to the heart.

Blood works hard all day! Eat good food. Drink lots of water, too. This helps keep blood healthy. In Saudi Arabia, drink water on hot days.

versions.title: Blood on the Move
versions.text:
Touch your wrist and hold still. Can you feel a beat? That beat is blood moving in you.

Your heart is a muscle. It pumps blood all day. It is about as big as your fist. It never stops.

Blood moves inside thin tubes. We call these tubes blood vessels. They go all through your body.

Some tubes carry blood away from the heart. We call these tubes arteries. They have strong, thick walls.

Other tubes carry blood back to the heart. We call these tubes veins. Their walls are thinner.

The smallest tubes are capillaries. They are as thin as a hair. Here blood gives food and oxygen to cells. It also picks up waste.

Blood goes to your lungs too. There it gets fresh oxygen. Then it flows back to your heart.

Your blood works hard all day and all night! Eating good food and drinking water helps it stay healthy. In Saudi Arabia, drink lots of water on hot days.

versions.title: The Busy Trip of Blood
versions.text:
Put your hand on your wrist and hold still. Can you feel a small beat? That beat means blood is moving inside your body.

Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood all day and all night, and it never stops.

Blood moves inside thin tubes called blood vessels. These tubes go to every part of your body.

Some tubes carry blood away from the heart. We call these tubes arteries. They have strong, thick walls because blood pushes hard inside them.

Other tubes carry blood back to the heart. We call these tubes veins. Their walls are thinner than artery walls.

The smallest tubes in your body are capillaries. They are as thin as a hair. Here, blood gives oxygen and food to your cells, and it picks up waste too.

Blood also goes to your lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air. Then it flows back to your heart to start again.

Your blood works hard all day and all night! Eating good food and drinking enough water both help keep it healthy. In Saudi Arabia, it is smart to drink lots of water on hot days.

Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood all day and all night, and it never stops working.

Blood moves through a network of thin tubes called blood vessels. These vessels reach every part of your body.

Some vessels carry blood away from the heart out to the body. We call these vessels arteries. They have strong, thick walls because blood pushes hard inside them.

The smallest vessels in your body are capillaries. They are as thin as a single hair. Here, blood gives oxygen and nutrients to your cells, and it picks up waste to carry away.

Blood also travels to your lungs. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air you breathe. Then it flows back to your heart to start the trip again.

Your blood works hard every minute of the day, carrying what your body needs. Eating good food and drinking enough water both help keep your blood healthy. In Saudi Arabia, it is smart to drink lots of water on hot days.

versions.title: The Circulation of Blood
versions.text:
Place your hand on your wrist and hold still for a moment. Can you feel a small, steady beat? That beat means blood is moving through your body right now.

Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood all day and all night, and it never stops working.

Blood travels through a network of thin tubes called blood vessels. These vessels reach every part of your body, from your brain to your toes.

Some vessels, called arteries, carry blood away from the heart out to the body. They have strong, thick walls because blood pushes hard inside them with each heartbeat.

Other vessels, called veins, carry blood back to the heart once it has traveled around the body. Their walls are thinner than artery walls.

The smallest vessels in your body are capillaries. They are as thin as a single hair. Here, blood gives oxygen and nutrients to your cells, and it picks up waste to carry away.

Blood also travels to your lungs as it circulates around your body. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air you breathe, and it drops off waste gas called carbon dioxide. Then it flows back to your heart.

Your blood works hard every minute of the day, carrying what your body needs. Eating good food and drinking enough water both help keep your blood healthy. In Saudi Arabia, where summer days get hot, it is smart to drink plenty of water.

versions.title: The Circulation of Blood
versions.text:
Place your hand on your wrist and remain still for a moment. Can you feel a small, steady beat? That beat means blood is circulating through your body right now, pushed along by your heart.

Your heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist. It pumps blood day and night without ever stopping, even while you are fast asleep, delivering it to every part of your body.

Blood travels through an enormous network of thin tubes called blood vessels, which reach every part of your body, from your brain down to the tips of your toes.

Some vessels, called arteries, carry blood away from your heart out to the rest of your body. Arteries have strong, thick walls because the blood pushes hard inside them with every heartbeat.

Other vessels, called veins, carry blood back toward your heart once it has traveled around the body. Veins have thinner walls than arteries because the blood moves through them more gently and at lower pressure.

The tiniest vessels in your body are called capillaries, and they are thinner than a single hair. Inside these tiny tubes, blood passes oxygen and nutrients from your food to your cells, and it collects waste from the cells to carry away.

Blood also travels to your lungs during its circulation around the body. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air you breathe in, and it releases a waste gas called carbon dioxide. Then it flows back to your heart to begin the entire trip again.

Your blood works hard every single minute of the day, carrying what your body needs and removing what it does not need. Eating healthy food and drinking enough water both help keep your blood, heart, and vessels healthy. In Saudi Arabia, where summer days can be extremely hot, it is wise to drink plenty of water throughout the day.

Place your hand on your wrist and remain completely still for a moment. Can you detect a small, steady beat? That beat indicates that blood is circulating through your body right now, propelled along by your heart.

Your heart is a muscular organ approximately the size of your fist, and together with your blood vessels it forms your cardiovascular system. It contracts continuously, day and night, even while you are fast asleep, pumping blood to every part of your body.

Blood travels through an extensive network of tubes called blood vessels, which extend to every part of your body, from your brain down to the tips of your toes.

Some vessels, known as arteries, carry blood away from your heart out to the rest of your body. Arteries have strong, thick, elastic walls because the blood pushes forcefully inside them each time the heart contracts.

Other vessels, known as veins, carry blood back toward your heart once it has traveled around the body. Veins have thinner walls than arteries because the blood moves through them more gently and at a much lower pressure.

Blood also travels to your lungs along a shorter pulmonary route within its circulation around the body. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air you breathe in, and it releases carbon dioxide, a waste gas, so you can exhale it. Then it flows back to your heart to begin the entire journey again.

Your blood works hard every single minute of the day, continuously carrying what your body needs and removing what it does not need. versions.title: How Blood Travels Through the Body
versions.text:
Placing a hand on the wrist and remaining completely still for a moment typically reveals a small, steady beat. This beat is evidence that blood is circulating continuously through the body, propelled along by the rhythmic action of the heart.

The heart is a muscular organ approximately the size of a fist, and together with the extensive network of blood vessels it forms the cardiovascular system, which contracts continuously, day and night, even throughout sleep, pumping blood to every part of the body without pause.

Blood travels through an extensive and branching network of tubes called blood vessels, which extend to every part of the body, from the delicate tissue of the brain down to the tips of the toes.

Some vessels, known as arteries, carry blood away from the heart out to the rest of the body. Arteries have strong, thick, elastic walls because blood is pushed forcefully inside them each time the heart contracts.

Other vessels, known as veins, carry blood back toward the heart once it has traveled around the body. Veins have considerably thinner walls than arteries because blood moves through them more gently, at a much lower pressure, often assisted by the squeezing of nearby muscles as a person moves.

The tiniest vessels in the body, called capillaries, are thinner than a single strand of hair, and it is inside these minuscule tubes that red blood cells release oxygen, carried by a protein called hemoglobin, along with nutrients absorbed from food, directly to the surrounding cells, while simultaneously collecting carbon dioxide and other waste to carry away.

Blood also travels to the lungs along a shorter pulmonary route within its overall circulation around the body. There it picks up fresh oxygen from the air that is inhaled and releases carbon dioxide, a waste gas, so that it can be exhaled, before flowing back to the heart to begin the entire journey again.

The blood works tirelessly every single minute of the day, continuously carrying what the body needs and removing what it does not need. Eating nutritious food and drinking sufficient water both help keep the cardiovascular system healthy throughout a lifetime. In Saudi Arabia, where summer days can be extremely hot, it remains wise to drink plenty of water throughout the day.

versions.title: How Blood Travels Through the Body
versions.text:
Placing a hand against the wrist and remaining entirely motionless for a moment will typically reveal a small, steady pulsation, tangible evidence that blood is circulating through the body, propelled continuously along by the heart.

The heart is a muscular organ approximately the size of a clenched fist, and together with the blood vessels it constitutes the cardiovascular system, which contracts continuously, day and night, even throughout sleep, pumping blood to every part of the body without interruption.

Blood travels through an extensive and intricately branching network of tubes called blood vessels, which extend to every part of the body, from the delicate tissues of the brain down to the most distal tips of the toes.

Some vessels, known as arteries, carry blood away from the heart out toward the rest of the body, and arteries possess strong, thick, elastic walls because the blood is forced through them with considerable pressure each time the heart contracts.

Other vessels, known as veins, carry blood back toward the heart once it has completed its journey around the body. Veins have considerably thinner walls than arteries because the blood moves through them more gently and at a much lower pressure, often assisted by the rhythmic contraction of nearby skeletal muscles.

The tiniest vessels in the body are called capillaries, thinner than a single strand of hair, and it is within these minuscule tubes that red blood cells release oxygen, transported by a specialized protein called hemoglobin, along with nutrients absorbed from digested food, directly to the surrounding cells, while the capillaries simultaneously collect carbon dioxide and other metabolic waste from those cells to carry away.

Blood also travels to the lungs along a shorter pulmonary route within its overall circulation around the body, where it picks up fresh oxygen from the air that has been inhaled and releases carbon dioxide, a waste gas, so that it can subsequently be exhaled, before flowing back to the heart to begin the entire journey once again.

The blood works tirelessly every single minute of every day, continuously delivering what the body requires and removing what it no longer needs, whether a person is a growing child, a busy adult, or an elderly grandparent. Eating nutritious food and drinking sufficient water both help keep the cardiovascular system healthy throughout an entire lifetime, and in Saudi Arabia, where summer days can become extraordinarily hot, it remains wise to drink plenty of water throughout the day, both indoors and outdoors.

versions.title: How Blood Travels Through the Body
versions.text:
Placing a hand against the wrist and remaining entirely motionless for a moment will typically reveal a small, steady pulsation, tangible evidence that blood is circulating ceaselessly through the body, propelled continuously along by the heart's rhythmic action.

The heart, a muscular organ approximately comparable in dimension to a clenched fist, together with the extensive network of blood vessels through which it propels blood, constitutes the cardiovascular system, a physiological apparatus that contracts continuously, day and night, even throughout the unconscious hours of sleep, pumping blood to every part of the body without a single interruption.

Blood must travel through an extensive and intricately branching network of tubes called blood vessels, which extend to every individual part of the body, from the delicate neural tissue of the brain down to the most distal tips of the toes.

Some vessels, known as arteries, carry blood away from the heart out toward the rest of the body, and arteries possess strong, thick, elastic walls precisely because blood is forced through them under considerable pressure each time the heart contracts.

Other vessels, known as veins, carry blood back toward the heart once it has completed its journey around the body; veins have considerably thinner walls than arteries because blood moves through them more gently and at a substantially lower pressure, often assisted by the rhythmic contraction of nearby skeletal muscles.

The tiniest vessels in the body are called capillaries, thinner than a single strand of hair, and it is within these minuscule tubes that red blood cells release oxygen, transported by a specialized protein called hemoglobin, along with nutrients absorbed from digested food, directly to the surrounding cells, while the capillaries simultaneously collect carbon dioxide and other metabolic waste products from those cells to carry away.

Blood also travels to the lungs along a comparatively shorter pulmonary route within its overall circulation around the body, where it picks up fresh oxygen from the air that has been inhaled and releases carbon dioxide, a waste gas, so that it can subsequently be exhaled, before flowing back to the heart to begin the entire journey once again.

The blood works tirelessly every single minute of every day, continuously delivering what the body requires and removing what it no longer needs, regardless of whether the person it serves is a growing child, a busy working adult, or an elderly grandparent resting at home. Eating nutritious food and drinking sufficient water both help keep the cardiovascular system functioning well throughout an entire lifetime, and within Saudi Arabia, where summer temperatures can become extraordinarily elevated, it remains advisable to drink plenty of water throughout the day, both indoors and outdoors.

a tube that carries blood

wrong.B: There is no story about a vacation.
wrong.D: The article names vessels, not the body's biggest organs.

MID.prompt: Explain how blood circulates through your body, using the words oxygen and nutrient. Describe at least three steps in the journey.
checklist: I described at least three steps in the blood's journey.
I used the words oxygen and nutrient correctly.
I explained what happens in the capillaries.
MID.modelAnswer: Blood circulates by first being pumped out of the heart through arteries, which carry it to the rest of my body. In the tiny capillaries, the blood delivers oxygen and nutrients from my food to my cells, and it picks up waste at the same time. The blood then flows back through veins to my heart, and some of it travels to my lungs to pick up fresh oxygen before the whole trip begins again.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the heart and the blood vessels
keyWords.example: Doctors say swimming is excellent for cardiovascular health.

keyWords.definition: to squeeze or tighten, becoming smaller
keyWords.example: A muscle must contract before it can lift something heavy.

keyWords.definition: a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen
keyWords.example: A blood test can measure how much hemoglobin a person has.

keyWords.definition: a gas made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, often a waste gas from the body
keyWords.example: Plants use carbon dioxide from the air to grow.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the lungs
keyWords.example: A pulmonary specialist is a doctor who treats lung problems.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The cardiovascular system functions only during vigorous exercise, and it rests when a person sits or sleeps, so the heart stops for hours at a time
Veins and arteries are identical in structure and function, and blood travels in only one kind of vessel, which has no valves, from the heart back to the heart
Capillaries are the body's largest blood vessels, and they carry most of the blood away from the heart and the lungs to the arms and legs of a person
The cardiovascular system continuously circulates blood through vessels, delivering oxygen and nutrients and removing waste, including a pulmonary circuit to the lungs
questions.why: The article describes how the cardiovascular system constantly moves blood through arteries, veins, and capillaries, including a route to the lungs.

wrong.A: The article says the heart works continuously, day and night, not only during exercise.
wrong.B: Arteries and veins are described as having different wall thickness and pressure.
wrong.C: Capillaries are described as the tiniest vessels, thinner than a hair.

questions.stem: What protein carries oxygen inside red blood cells?
options: Nutrient
Hemoglobin
Capillarin
Plasma fiber
questions.why: The article names hemoglobin as the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells.

wrong.A: A nutrient is something from food, not an oxygen-carrying protein.
wrong.C: Capillarin is not a real term used in the article.
wrong.D: Plasma fiber is not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: Which vessels have the thickest, most elastic walls?
options: Arteries
Veins
Capillaries
Lymph tubes
questions.why: In the article, arteries have strong, thick, elastic walls because blood is forced through them under pressure.

wrong.B: Veins have considerably thinner walls than arteries.
wrong.C: Capillaries are described as thinner than a single strand of hair.
wrong.D: Lymph tubes are not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: In the article, the word pulmonary refers to something related to the —
options: bones
muscles
lungs
skin
questions.why: The article describes a pulmonary route that carries blood to the lungs.

wrong.A: Bones are not discussed in connection with the pulmonary route.
wrong.B: Skeletal muscles are mentioned separately, for helping veins.
wrong.D: Skin is not connected to the word pulmonary in the article.

questions.stem: Why do arteries need strong, elastic walls?
options: Because they are the thinnest vessels in the body, so the blood needs a strong cover
Because they carry the least amount of blood, so they must be strong and stiff
Because they only work during sleep, when the body needs the most blood at once
Because blood is forced through them under high pressure each time the heart contracts
questions.why: In the article, arteries need strong walls because blood pushes through them with pressure every time the heart contracts.

wrong.A: Capillaries, not arteries, are the thinnest vessels.
wrong.B: Arteries carry blood pumped straight from the heart, not the least amount.
wrong.C: The heart works continuously, including during sleep.

questions.stem: A patient's doctor explains that their tissue is not getting enough oxygen. Which part of the cardiovascular system is most directly responsible for delivering oxygen to tissue?
options: Capillaries
The heart's outer wall
The lungs' outer surface
The skin
questions.why: The article explains that oxygen passes from blood to cells inside the tiny capillaries, so a problem there would stop oxygen from reaching tissue.

wrong.B: The heart's outer wall is not described as delivering oxygen to body tissue.
wrong.C: The lungs exchange gases with the air, not directly with body tissue.
wrong.D: The skin is not described as delivering oxygen to the body's tissue.

questions.stem: How do veins compare with arteries, according to the article?
options: Veins carry only carbon dioxide, never oxygen, from the body to the heart
Veins have thinner walls and carry blood at a lower pressure than arteries
Veins are located only inside the lungs, where they meet the air
Veins pump blood by contracting like the heart, with thick walls
questions.why: The article contrasts veins and arteries, explaining that veins have thinner walls and lower blood pressure.

wrong.A: The article does not say veins carry only carbon dioxide.
wrong.C: Veins are found throughout the body, not only in the lungs.
wrong.D: Only the heart is described as contracting to pump blood.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain the pulmonary route separately from the rest of circulation?
options: To argue that the lungs are not part of the body, because they only help with breathing and have no link to blood
To prove that the heart does not pump blood to the lungs, since the lungs make their own blood supply
To show that blood takes a shorter, separate trip to the lungs to exchange gases before continuing around the body
To compare the lungs in children and adults, showing that a child's lungs are much smaller in size
questions.why: The article sets apart the pulmonary route to show it is a shorter side trip for gas exchange within the larger circulation.

wrong.A: The article treats the lungs as an important part of the body's circulation.
wrong.B: The heart is described as pumping blood to the lungs along this route.
wrong.D: No comparison between children and adults is made.

HIGH.prompt: Explain the full path a red blood cell takes, starting and ending at the heart, including its trip through the pulmonary route. Use at least three key words from this article.
checklist: I described the full loop, starting and ending at the heart.
I explained what happens in the pulmonary route.
I used at least three key words from the article correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A red blood cell leaves the heart through an artery after the heart contracts, traveling through the cardiovascular system to reach the capillaries, where hemoglobin releases oxygen and nutrients to the body's cells while collecting carbon dioxide. The cell then returns through a vein to the heart, which sends it on the shorter pulmonary route to the lungs, where it drops off carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen before beginning the entire journey again.

LOW.stem: How can you feel that blood is moving in your body?
options: By pressing on your stomach
By touching your wrist
By touching your teeth
By holding your breath
LOW.why: In the article, to touch your wrist and feel a beat, which is blood.

wrong.A: The article never mentions the stomach.
wrong.C: The article never mentions teeth.
wrong.D: Holding your breath is not in the article.

LOW.stem: In the article, the word pumps means —
options: holds blood still
makes blood cold
turns blood to water
pushes blood along
LOW.why: The heart pumps blood so that it moves through the tubes in the body.

wrong.A: Blood is always moving, not held still.
wrong.B: The article does not say the heart cools blood.
wrong.C: Blood does not turn into water.

LOW.stem: Why does the author say capillaries are as thin as a hair?
options: To show they are very small
To show they are very strong
To show they are very hot
To show they are very long
LOW.why: Comparing capillaries to a hair shows that they are tiny tubes.

wrong.B: Thin things are not described as strong here.
wrong.C: Heat has nothing to do with the hair comparison.
wrong.D: The comparison is about width, not length.

LOW.stem: What does blood do right after it gets fresh air in the lungs?
options: It turns into trash
It stops moving
It goes back to the heart
It leaves through the wrist
LOW.why: The article says blood gets fresh air in the lungs and then goes back to the heart.

wrong.A: Blood does not turn into trash.
wrong.B: Blood never stops moving.
wrong.D: Blood stays inside the body tubes.

MID.stem: What waste gas does blood drop off in the lungs?
options: Oxygen
Water
Carbon dioxide
Nutrients
MID.why: In the article, blood drops off a waste gas called carbon dioxide in the lungs.

wrong.A: Oxygen is picked up in the lungs, not dropped off.
wrong.B: Water is not named as the waste gas.
wrong.D: Nutrients are given to cells, not dropped in the lungs.

MID.stem: In the article, the word network means —
options: a group of joined tubes
a single tube in the heart
a kind of food for cells
a loud beat at the wrist
MID.why: Blood vessels reach every part of the body, so they form a joined system.

wrong.B: There are many vessels, not one tube.
wrong.C: A network is not a food.
wrong.D: The beat is felt at the wrist, but that is not a network.

MID.stem: Why do blood vessels need to reach from your brain to your toes?
options: Only the brain needs blood
Every body part needs blood
The toes make the blood hot
The heart is in the toes
MID.why: Blood carries oxygen and nutrients, so vessels must reach all body parts.

wrong.A: In the article, vessels reach every part of the body.
wrong.C: The article does not say toes heat the blood.
wrong.D: The heart is the size of a fist, not in the toes.

MID.stem: Why does the author start by asking you to feel your wrist?
options: To teach you how to count
To show blood is moving now
To tell you your wrist is weak
To explain how to cut a finger
MID.why: The beat at your wrist means blood is moving, which makes the topic real for the reader.

wrong.A: Counting is not part of the article.
wrong.C: The wrist is not called weak.
wrong.D: Cutting a finger is not in this article.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, what do capillaries collect from your cells?
options: Hemoglobin and protein
Nutrients and food
Fresh oxygen from the air
Carbon dioxide and waste
HIGH.why: The article says capillaries collect carbon dioxide and other waste from cells.

wrong.A: Hemoglobin carries oxygen and is not collected from cells.
wrong.B: Nutrients are delivered to cells, not collected from them.
wrong.C: Fresh oxygen comes from the lungs.

HIGH.stem: The article describes the blood vessels as an extensive network. What does extensive mean here?
options: very old and weak
hidden below the heart
wide-reaching and large
short and straight
HIGH.why: The vessels extend to every part of the body, from the brain to the toes, so extensive means wide-reaching.

wrong.A: Age and weakness are not discussed.
wrong.B: The vessels reach all of the body, not just below the heart.
wrong.D: Vessels extend far and are not described as short.

HIGH.stem: The article says the heart contracts day and night, even during sleep. What can you conclude from this?
options: The body always needs blood
The heart is only strong at night
Sleeping makes the blood thicker
Arteries rest when you sleep
HIGH.why: If the heart keeps pumping during sleep, the body must need blood all the time.

wrong.B: The article says the heart works day and night.
wrong.C: Blood thickness is not discussed.
wrong.D: The article says the heart never stops, so blood keeps moving.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author end with a sentence about summer days in Saudi Arabia?
options: To say summer makes blood vessels grow
To link the health advice to the reader's own life
To explain how the lungs work in the heat
To compare Saudi Arabia with other countries
HIGH.why: The author ties the advice about drinking water to the hot weather readers in Saudi Arabia know well.

wrong.A: Vessels growing in summer is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The sentence is about drinking water, not the lungs.
wrong.D: No other countries are compared.
